text: Security Incident Response. A breach, a phishing report, detected malware — these need a dedicated application, not a regular Incident record with a scarier label, and this lesson explains exactly why.

A regular Incident asks what's broken and how fast can we restore service. A Security Incident asks a completely different question: has this organization been compromised, who did it, what did they touch, and what does the law now require us to do about it. A printer outage and a confirmed phishing campaign that just harvested forty employees' credentials are not the same kind of problem, even though both could technically be logged as an incident.

How it's built on the platform is nothing new to you. Security Incident Response extends the task table the same way any specialized application does, inheriting short description, assignment group, state, and work notes. What's different is the workflow layered on top. A regular Incident moves New, In Progress, Resolved, Closed. A Security Incident moves through Analysis, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, and Review.

Containment comes first, deliberately before you've fully understood the threat — isolating an infected endpoint, disabling a compromised account, blocking a malicious IP, right now, before the damage keeps growing. Eradication comes next: actually removing the root cause, not just the symptom you contained — the malware itself, the vulnerability that let the attacker in, the stolen credentials. Recovery comes last: restoring normal operation only once you have real confidence the threat is gone.

The order is the whole point. Reconnecting a cleaned-looking endpoint before eradication is actually finished just puts a still-infected system back on the network — exactly the mistake this phase model exists to prevent.

And a Security Incident carries weight a regular Incident never does. Its work notes may become evidence, read by legal counsel, a regulator, or a cyber-insurance carrier. Certain categories — a confirmed breach involving personal data — can trigger notification obligations that simply don't exist for an outage ticket. That's why this isn't Incident Management with a scarier name: the record lives inside a different set of obligations from the moment it opens. And it isn't really finished when service is restored — the post-incident review, what happened, how it was caught, what should change, is what makes the whole exercise organizational learning instead of one-off firefighting.
Containment, eradication, recovery, then review — in that order, for a reason. Next up: Vulnerability Response, which exists to catch the next incident before it becomes one at all.
